practice_items.prompt: An email says 'Your account closes in 1 hour unless you verify now.' Which tactic is this PRIMARILY using?
practice_items.explain: Manufactured time pressure ('1 hour', 'now') is urgency; it pushes you to act before verifying. It is not scarcity, because nothing is described as limited in supply, and nobody claims special authority.

practice_items.prompt: A message reads: 'This is the IRS. Pay the penalty within 24 hours or face arrest.' Select ALL tactics present.
practice_items.explain: IRS = authority, '24 hours' = urgency, 'penalty'/'arrest' = intimidation. No scarcity.

practice_items.prompt: Why is recognizing the underlying TACTIC more useful than memorizing specific scam templates?
options: Scam templates are copyrighted, so security training cannot show real examples
Tactics stay constant even when attackers change the brand, wording, or channel
Spam filters already catch every known template, so only tactics are left to learn
Each tactic appears in only one kind of scam, so naming it identifies the scam
practice_items.explain: Surface details (brand, wording, channel, even AI-written text) change constantly, but the psychological levers do not, so recognizing the lever generalizes to messages you have never seen. Filters do not catch every template, and tactics are not tied to one scam type: urgency shows up in bank, IRS and CEO scams alike.

practice_items.prompt: Name the single best defensive response when you notice manufactured emotional pressure in a message.
practice_items.explain: Slow down and verify the request through a separate, trusted channel.

practice_items.prompt: An attacker tells a receptionist 'I heard your VPN uses port 1433, or was it 443?' hoping the receptionist corrects them. Which elicitation gambit is this?
practice_items.explain: Stating something wrong to provoke a correction is the deliberate-incorrect-statement gambit. The target volunteers the accurate detail to fix the error.

practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are malicious indicators in the URL http://paypa1.com/verify.exe ? Select ALL that apply.
options: mismatched-link (the link text differs from where it really goes)
ip-url (the host is a numeric address)
practice_items.explain: paypa1.com swaps the letter l for the digit 1, so it is a lookalike domain, and verify.exe downloads a program. There is no separate link text shown here to compare against, so mismatched-link cannot be judged, and the host is a name, not an IP address.

practice_items.prompt: A filename shows as 'invoice.pdf' in Windows Explorer. When you look at the true name it is 'invoice.pdf.exe'. What technique does this use?
practice_items.explain: A double extension exploits Windows hiding known extensions by default, making .exe appear as .pdf in the file browser.

practice_items.prompt: Why does HTTPS in a URL NOT prove that a website is safe?
practice_items.explain: HTTPS only proves the connection is encrypted. Attackers freely obtain TLS certificates for malicious domains; the padlock does not mean the site is legitimate.

practice_items.prompt: Which action BEST defends against elicitation when someone you do not recognize asks detailed questions about your network?
options: Answer only general questions and refuse anything specific
Ask them a security question only a real employee would know
Verify their identity through official channels before sharing any operational details
Share only details that are already on the company website
practice_items.explain: Elicitation works by collecting small, harmless-seeming pieces, so "general" or "public" answers still help the attacker build a picture, and a quiz question can be researched or guessed. Verifying identity through an official channel (a directory number, the security team) before sharing anything is the reliable defense.

practice_items.atom_title: Email, text, and social media attacks
practice_items.prompt: An attacker registers 'paypa1.com' (digit 1 replacing the letter l) and sends password-reset emails from that domain. Which technique does this PRIMARILY represent?
practice_items.explain: Substituting visually similar characters in a domain name to impersonate a trusted brand is a lookalike (homograph) domain attack, the core technique behind most phishing sender spoofing.

practice_items.atom_title: Email, text, and social media attacks
practice_items.prompt: A text message says: 'UPS: Your package is held. Reschedule at http://bit.ly/upsdel.' What makes SMS (smishing) especially effective for this type of attack?
options: SMS messages cannot be filtered by spam engines
Limited screen real estate hides full URLs; people trust texts on personal devices
Phones display URLs in full without truncation
SMS is encrypted end-to-end so attackers can bypass firewalls
practice_items.explain: Smishing exploits the fact that phone screens show truncated or shortened URLs and that people have higher baseline trust in SMS messages received on personal devices.

practice_items.atom_title: Email, text, and social media attacks
practice_items.prompt: A social media DM says: 'Your account expires tonight. Verify at http://192.168.5.1/login to avoid losing access.' Select ALL phishing indicators present.
options: Shortened link / bare IP address URL
Credential request (verify to avoid losing access)
practice_items.explain: The bare IP address URL triggers the shortened-link indicator, 'expires tonight' is urgency, and 'verify to avoid losing access' is a credential request. A legitimate organization does not send you to a bare IP address.

practice_items.atom_title: Email, text, and social media attacks
practice_items.prompt: What distinguishes spear phishing from generic phishing?
options: Spear phishing is sent by text message, while phishing is sent by email
Spear phishing always carries malware, while phishing only steals passwords
Spear phishing targets executives, while phishing targets ordinary employees
Spear phishing uses pre-researched details about a specific target to increase believability
practice_items.explain: The defining feature is research: spear phishing is tailored to one person or group using details like their name, role and recent activity. It can use any channel and any payload. Phishing aimed at executives specifically has its own name, whaling, which is a subtype of spear phishing.

practice_items.atom_title: Email, text, and social media attacks
practice_items.prompt: Name the one defensive action that works across email, SMS, and social media phishing when you suspect a message is fraudulent.
practice_items.explain: Verify through an independent channel, look up the organization's real contact information separately and reach out that way, rather than using any link, number, or address in the suspicious message.
